tagline: North under the cedars to the potters of Seagrove.
intro: NC 705 starts at Eagle Springs, on NC 211 between Candor and Pinehurst, and runs north under the old cedars locals call Cedar Lane. It passes through Robbins and on through Whynot into Seagrove, which was to be Seagraves, for a railroad man, until, the story goes, the sign painter ran short of room.

Potters have worked this clay since the 18th century. The trade was nearly gone when Jacques and Juliana Busbee of Raleigh traced an orange pie dish to Moore County and set local potters to work for a shop in Greenwich Village. Later the road to Pinehurst brought tourists past, and some families here are eighth- and ninth-generation potters.

moments.title: Robbins
moments.text: A gunsmith's rifle works made this Mechanics Hill, the railroad made it Elise, and in 1943 the legislature renamed it for Karl Robbins, who had bought the local textile mill.

moments.title: Jugtown
moments.text: When the Busbees' pottery went on the National Register in 1999, the listing took in its log sales room, log turning room and two kilns under a shelter, all built about 1921.

moments.title: Whynot
moments.text: Residents arguing over a name got this one when a man finally said, why not name the town Why Not and let's go home.
